meta.title: ai-jail compared with built-in agent sandboxes, Docker and VMs
meta.description: What the sandboxes in Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI cover, what they leave outside, where they beat ai-jail, and how Docker, VMs and NVIDIA OpenShell compare, with sources.

hero.title: Your agent already has a sandbox. It covers a different half.
hero.lede: Built-in sandboxes and permission prompts watch the commands the model runs. ai-jail decides what the whole agent program can see on your machine. The two work together.
hero.reviewed: Last reviewed {date}. Other products change quickly, so every claim about them links to the vendor's own documentation.

wall.title: Where the wall is
wall.lede: At the time of writing, Claude Code's sandbox applies to shell commands and their child processes. Its file tools use the permission system instead, and its documentation says MCP servers and hooks run unconstrained on the host. ai-jail starts the agent itself inside the wall, so everything it launches is inside too.
wall.alt: Two panels. On the left a built-in sandbox encloses only the shell commands, while the agent, its MCP servers and its hooks sit outside the wall with lines reaching your home directory. On the right ai-jail encloses the agent, MCP servers, hooks, shell commands and the project together, and your home directory is outside, dim and barred.
wall.caption: The left panel follows Claude Code's documentation.
wall.codex: Codex also sandboxes the commands it spawns and leaves the codex process outside. Its documentation does not say where local MCP servers run.

prompts.title: A permission prompt is a different kind of protection
prompts.lede: A prompt asks a person, and a person can be rushed or fooled. A sandbox asks the kernel, which gives the same answer every time.
prompts.alt: Two panels. On the left a line from the agent passes through a stack of approval dialogs with an Approve button and reaches your keys. On the right the same line stops at a wall labeled kernel rule, and your keys behind it are dim and barred.
prompts.caption: Prompts are useful. They are a review step, and a sandbox is a boundary.
prompts.modesTitle: Modes that take the person out
prompts.modesNote: At the time of writing, each of these agents has a mode that stops asking. When the prompt is gone, the sandbox is the only protection left, if one is on.

cols.effect: What the vendor says it does

modes.effect: Everything runs and a second model reviews actions in your place. The documentation calls this classifier a per-action control, not an isolation boundary.
Everything runs with no checks. The documentation says to use it in isolated containers and VMs only.
The agent never asks. The sandbox mode still applies. See approvals and security.
The sandbox is off. With --yolo there are no approvals either.

table.title: Side by side
table.lede: Everything here describes each product's documentation at the time of writing. Where the documentation we read does not answer a question, the cell says so.
table.sources: Sources: Claude Code sandboxing, Claude Code sandbox environments, Codex approvals and security, Codex Linux sandbox, Gemini CLI sandbox.
table.groupJail: What a wrapper around the whole agent adds
table.groupBuiltin: What the built-in sandboxes do better

rows.label: What is inside the wall
cells: Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands and their children. The claude process, its file tools, MCP servers and hooks are outside.
The commands the agent spawns. The codex process is outside. Local MCP servers: not documented.
The whole CLI process, or only the shell and write tools with security.toolSandboxing.
The whole process tree: the agent, its file tools, MCP servers, hooks and every command.

rows.label: On by default
cells: No. You turn it on with /sandbox or sandbox.enabled. If a dependency is missing it warns and runs commands unsandboxed, unless you set sandbox.failIfUnavailable.
Yes. workspace-write is the default mode.
You turn it on with -s, GEMINI_SANDBOX or tools.sandbox.
It is on whenever you start the agent through it. If the configuration is invalid it refuses to start.

rows.label: Can sandboxed code read ~/.ssh by default?
cells: Yes. The documentation says the default still allows reading credential files such as ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh/. Deny rules are opt-in.
Yes on Linux, where the whole filesystem is mounted read only. Deny entries are opt-in. macOS default: not documented.
The default macOS profile, permissive-open, allows broad file reads. Stricter profiles are opt-in.
No. The agent gets a fresh, empty home directory. --ssh is an opt-in.

rows.label: Environment variables
cells: Sandboxed commands inherit the parent environment by default, credentials included. sandbox.credentials can deny or mask them.
A minimal allowlist of terminal, locale and toolchain variables. You add others by name with --env.

rows.label: Escape hatch the model can use
cells: The model may retry a command with dangerouslyDisableSandbox, which goes through the normal permission flow. allowUnsandboxedCommands: false turns that off.
With the on-request policy the agent asks to leave the sandbox for edits outside the workspace or for network.
None. You set the policy before the agent starts, and a project's own .ai-jail file can tighten it but never open it.

rows.label: Works with every agent
cells: Claude Code only
Codex only
Gemini CLI only
Any command, with one policy file for all of your agents.

rows.label: Network model
cells: A proxy with a per-domain allowlist. A new domain prompts you, and each command still gets its own approval. The documentation notes that the proxy trusts the hostname the client sends, so domain fronting can bypass it.
Off by default in workspace-write. One setting turns it on, and an optional proxy adds per-domain allow and deny rules. The documentation says the proxy does not filter MCP server connections.
The default profile allows network. Stricter and proxied profiles are opt-in.

Three modes, off by default. --allow-host allows the listed hosts and their subdomains, enforced by the network namespace on Linux or a seatbelt endpoint rule on macOS, through a proxy that resolves each name once and dials the address it checked. --network opens everything. The filter is TCP only, has no per-path rules and never prompts: a host outside the list is denied and --audit-log records the attempt. An allowed host is trusted wholesale.

rows.label: Approval for each command
cells: Yes. Permission modes, a plan mode, a classifier model and managed organization policy.
Yes. Approval policies, per-category rules and an optional reviewer agent.
None. ai-jail never sees individual commands and never asks.

rows.label: Protected paths inside the project
cells: Yes. .git/hooks, .git/config, .claude settings, .mcp.json, shell rc files and more stay read only.
Yes. .git, .agents and .codex under writable roots are read only.
None built in. The whole project is writable. You mask or deny paths yourself with --mask and deny_paths.

rows.label: Hiding secrets from the agent while still using them
cells: Credential masking can inject the real secret at the proxy. It needs an experimental setting.
No. A masked file is an empty file.

rows.label: Platforms
cells: macOS, Linux, WSL2. Not native Windows or WSL1.
macOS, Linux, WSL2 and native Windows.
macOS Seatbelt, Docker or Podman, gVisor, LXC (experimental) and native Windows.
Linux and macOS. On Windows, WSL2 only.

rows.label: Install
cells: Ships with the agent. On Linux it needs bubblewrap and socat.
Ships with the agent.
Ships with the agent. The container backends need Docker or Podman.
A separate binary. On Linux it needs bubblewrap.

table.runtimeTitle: Anthropic also ships a whole-process wrapper
table.runtimeText: At the time of writing, npx @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime claude wraps the whole Claude Code process with the same Seatbelt and bubblewrap primitives, so file tools, MCP servers and hooks are covered too. Anthropic describes it as a beta research preview, and notes that on Linux its deny list is built once at launch and does not cover files created later. If you only use Claude Code, it is a direct alternative to ai-jail.
table.opencodeTitle: OpenCode has rules and no sandbox
table.opencodeText: At the time of writing, OpenCode's permissions page documents allow, ask and deny rules, says most permissions default to allow, and does not describe an OS sandbox.

both.title: Use both
both.lede: With the network off, a cloud agent cannot reach its own model API. You open two things: the model's host and the agent's login. Allow one host, or open the whole network.
both.codeNote: ai-jail knows the API host of Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI, and warns at launch when the list does not include it. Every flag is on Configure.
both.alt: One large wall labeled ai-jail encloses the agent, its MCP servers, its hooks, the project and its shell commands. Between the agent and the shell commands sits the agent's own approval prompt. One line leaves the wall through a gate to the model API. Your home directory is outside the wall, dim and barred.
both.caption: The outer wall is ai-jail. Inside it, the agent's prompts and rules keep doing their job.

points.title: What the agent's own checks still do
points.text: Permission prompts, allow and deny rules and plan mode are part of the agent program, so they work inside the jail as they do outside. They catch the command you would not have approved.

points.title: What ai-jail guarantees underneath
points.text: The agent, its MCP servers and its hooks never see your home directory, your keys or the tokens in your shell, whatever you approve. What the agent can read, it can still send to any host you allowed, so mask the secrets inside the project.

both.nestedTitle: Keep the prompts, but do not count on a sandbox inside a sandbox
both.nestedText: On Linux, ai-jail blocks the system calls that create new namespaces and mounts, such as unshare and mount, because they are how a process escapes. A bubblewrap sandbox started by the agent inside the jail needs those calls, and the ai-jail documentation does not say that this combination works. Claude Code's documentation, at the time of writing, offers enableWeakerNestedSandbox for nested setups and says it considerably weakens security.

heavy.title: Docker, dev containers and virtual machines
heavy.lede: These are good answers too, and a virtual machine is a stronger one. They differ in what you have to build and keep up to date.

rows.gives: Its own filesystem, process list and network. The agent sees only what you mount.
rows.costs: An image to build and maintain, with your toolchains installed a second time. If you mount the Docker socket, the container is root-equivalent on the host.

rows.gives: The same isolation as a container, described in a file your editor understands and your team can share.
rows.costs: The same image upkeep, plus an editor or tool that understands the format.

rows.gives: Its own kernel. It is the strongest boundary here, and the right one for code you believe is hostile.
rows.costs: The heaviest option: a guest system to install, update, give memory to and copy your project into.

rows.gives: A sandbox around one command, using the compilers and runtimes already on your machine. It needs no image, daemon or root.
rows.costs: It shares your kernel, so a kernel or driver exploit is outside its boundary. It is weaker than a virtual machine.

heavy.note: ai-jail's own documentation calls it a useful layer, not a replacement for a disposable VM. Read the threat model.

platforms.title: Agent runtime platforms
platforms.lede: NVIDIA OpenShell is a different category: a running gateway that gives each agent its own container or MicroVM, with a policy engine in front of the network. ai-jail is one process that wraps one command and exits with it. This follows OpenShell's documentation at the time of writing, when it was still before its 1.0 release.

rows.label: What runs the sandbox
rows.openshell: A gateway daemon on Docker, Podman, Kubernetes or KVM. The agent lives in a bundled container image.
rows.jail: Nothing but the binary. The agent runs against your project with the compilers and runtimes already on your machine.

rows.label: Network
rows.openshell: Deny by default. Rules match program, host and port, with optional inspection of methods, paths and MCP tools. A denied endpoint can be approved from the operator's side.
rows.jail: Off, filtered by host, or open. The filter is a namespace fence and a CONNECT proxy; it sees hosts and ports but not content, and an allowed host is trusted wholesale.

rows.label: Credentials
rows.openshell: Brokered by the gateway and injected per request, never written to the sandbox disk.
rows.jail: Ambient. What you pass with --env, --env-from-file or --agent-state is visible to everything inside.

rows.label: Isolation ceiling
rows.openshell: A MicroVM driver gives a real virtual machine boundary, and sandboxes can stop, restart and keep their workspace.
rows.jail: Shares your kernel and is one-shot by design. For hostile code its own documentation says to use a disposable VM.

rows.label: macOS
rows.openshell: Runs inside the Docker Desktop Linux VM. The macOS host is outside the policy.
rows.jail: Native seatbelt profiles generated on the host.

rows.label: Telemetry and stability
rows.openshell: Anonymous telemetry on by default with an opt-out. The policy format is still changing.
rows.jail: No telemetry. Every new version keeps reading the configs older versions wrote, and tests enforce it.

platforms.note: The comparison in ai-jail's repository, docs/openshell-comparison.md, is written in both directions and is where the host allowlist came from.

items.q: Should I turn off my agent's own sandbox and prompts?
items.a: Keep the prompts and rules. They review single commands, which ai-jail never does. The agent's OS sandbox is a different matter on Linux: ai-jail blocks the system calls a nested bubblewrap sandbox needs, and its documentation does not say the combination works. If the agent reports that its sandbox is unavailable inside the jail, the jail is still there.

They are the same class of boundary. Both share your kernel, and neither is a virtual machine. ai-jail starts with everything closed and needs no image, no daemon and no root. A container mounts what you tell it to, and a mounted Docker socket is root-equivalent on the host. For code you believe is hostile, use a disposable VM.

items.q: How does the host allowlist differ from the agents' own?
items.a: The agents' proxies are something the sandboxed program has to choose to use. In ai-jail the fence is the kernel: on Linux the sandbox keeps a private network namespace whose only exit is the proxy, and on macOS a seatbelt rule allows outbound traffic to the proxy's port alone, so a program that ignores http_proxy reaches nothing. It does not cover UDP, so DNS inside the sandbox fails on Linux and the system resolver is not fenced on macOS, and it does not inspect the content of a connection, so an allowed host is trusted wholesale. It cannot combine with --network or --browser.

items.q: I only use Claude Code. Do I still need ai-jail?
items.a: You have three options, at the time of writing. The built-in sandbox covers shell commands. Anthropic's @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime, a beta research preview, wraps the whole process. ai-jail wraps the whole process too, starts with your home directory and environment variables closed, and uses the same policy for any other agent you try later. See Anthropic's comparison of sandbox environments.
